{"triples":[{"subject":"phonological theory","predicate":"uses","object":"logical transductions","object_type":"Other","source_sentence":"We can also fruitfully apply logical transductions to phonological theory (Heinz, forthcoming)."},{"subject":"generative","predicate":"addresses","object":"linguistic sound patterns","object_type":"Concept","source_sentence":"mainstream theories of generative phonology aim to explain linguistic sound patterns through a transformation from an input UR to an output SR."},{"subject":"rules","predicate":"uses","object":"finite state machines","object_type":"Other","source_sentence":"Johnson (1972) and Kaplan and Kay (1994) show that the phonological rewrite rules of Chomsky and Halle (1968) are describable with finite state machines; that is, that they describe Regular relations."},{"subject":"transformation","predicate":"addresses","object":"Regular string transductions","object_type":"Other","source_sentence":"Subsequent work on phonological transformations has demonstrated for a wide variety of processes —including local assimilation, deletion, and epenthesis ( Chandlee , 2014), dissimilation , metathesis ( Chandlee and Heinz, 2012), and vowel harmony —to lie in even more restrictive subclasses of Regular string transductions."},{"subject":"transformation","predicate":"addresses","object":"MSO-definable transductions","object_type":"Other","source_sentence":"From the logical perspective, all of these results place phonological transformations squarely within the class of MSO-definable transductions."}]}
